stem: A business owned and controlled by one person, who takes all the profit and bears all the risk, is a
options: cooperative society
partnership firm formed by one family
private limited company
sole proprietorship
explanation: In a sole proprietorship one person supplies the capital, manages the business and keeps all the profit or loss. A partnership needs at least two persons, even if they belong to one family.

stem: The liability of a sole proprietor for the debts of his business is
options: unlimited, so his private property can be used to pay them
limited to the value of the shop, its fittings and the stock held in it
shared equally with the business's creditors
limited to the capital he has put into the business
explanation: The law does not separate a sole trader from his business, so creditors can claim his personal assets if business assets are not enough. Liability limited to capital invested is a feature of shareholders in a limited company.

stem: Which of the following is a main advantage of a sole proprietorship?
options: quick decisions and close personal contact with customers
an unlimited supply of capital from the general public
a legal existence that continues after the owner's death
liability of the owner limited to the amount he has invested in the shop
explanation: A sole trader can decide at once without consulting anyone and knows his customers personally. Perpetual existence and limited liability belong to companies, and a sole trader cannot raise capital from the public.

stem: A major limitation of a sole proprietorship is
options: the need to share profits among many owners
limited capital and managing ability of one person
strict legal formalities and registration with the SECP for setting it up
the requirement to publish annual accounts
explanation: One person can raise only so much money and has limited time and skills, which restricts growth. A sole trader keeps all the profit, so profit sharing is not a limitation, and very few formalities are needed to start.

stem: The law governing partnership firms in Pakistan is the
options: Companies Act, 1932
Partnership Act, 1932
Partnership Ordinance, 1984
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
explanation: Partnerships in Pakistan are governed by the Partnership Act, 1932, inherited from the subcontinent's pre-independence law. The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 deals with cheques, bills and notes.

stem: The minimum number of persons needed to form a partnership is
options: one
three
two
seven
explanation: A partnership is a relation between persons who agree to share the profits of a business, so at least two persons are needed. A single owner forms a sole proprietorship.

stem: The written agreement that sets out the terms of a partnership, such as capital, profit-sharing ratio and duties, is the
options: memorandum of association
prospectus
partnership deed
articles of association
explanation: Partners record their terms in a partnership deed. The memorandum and articles of association are documents of a company, and a prospectus invites the public to buy a company's shares.

stem: If the partnership deed is silent on the matter, profits and losses are shared among the partners
options: equally, whatever their capital contributions
only by the active partners and not the others
in the ratio of the capital each partner contributed
in proportion to the hours each partner works
explanation: Under partnership law, when there is no agreement, partners share profits and losses equally. Sharing in the capital ratio is a common mistake: it applies only if the partners have agreed to it.

stem: A partner who contributes capital and shares profits but takes no part in running the business is a
options: active partner
minor partner
nominal partner
sleeping partner
explanation: A sleeping (dormant) partner invests and shares profits but does not take part in management; he is still liable to outsiders like other partners. A nominal partner lends only his name and usually invests no capital.

stem: A well-known person who allows his name to be used by a firm, but invests no capital and takes no share of profit, is a
options: secret partner
sleeping partner
working partner
nominal partner
explanation: A nominal partner lends his name and reputation only. A sleeping partner, by contrast, invests capital and shares profits.

stem: Under the Partnership Act, 1932, a minor
options: can be admitted to the benefits of partnership with the consent of all partners
can never receive any share in the profits of a firm
can become a full partner with unlimited personal liability
must be appointed as the managing partner of the firm by the other partners at once
explanation: A minor cannot enter into a contract, so he cannot be a full partner; with all partners' consent he may be admitted to the benefits of partnership, and his liability is limited to his share in the firm. He has no personal liability for the firm's debts while a minor.

stem: Under the Partnership Act, 1932, registration of a firm is
options: required only for firms with more than ten partners
optional, but an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties to enforce contracts
possible only after the firm has made its first profit
compulsory before the firm can begin any business at all
explanation: The Act does not make registration compulsory, but an unregistered firm and its partners lose the right to sue outsiders on the firm's contracts. It is not true that an unregistered firm cannot do business at all.

stem: "Mutual agency" in a partnership means that
options: each partner is an agent of the firm and of the other partners
partners must appoint an outside agent to manage the firm
the firm acts as a commission agent for other businesses in the same trade
a partner can act only after all others agree in writing
explanation: Every partner can bind the firm and the other partners by acts done in the ordinary course of business, and is bound by their acts too. This is why partners must trust one another.

stem: A partnership with no fixed period, which any partner can end by giving notice, is a
options: joint venture partnership
particular partnership
limited partnership
partnership at will
explanation: When the deed sets no time limit, the partnership is "at will" and may be dissolved by notice from any partner. A particular partnership is formed for one venture or a fixed period.

stem: The liability of partners in an ordinary partnership firm is
options: limited to the capital each partner contributed
unlimited and joint and several
borne only by the partner who caused the debt
limited to the amount stated in the partnership deed
explanation: Each partner is liable for all the firm's debts, both together and individually, so a creditor can recover the whole amount from any one partner. Limited liability is a company feature.

stem: A partnership firm is compulsorily dissolved when
options: the firm suffers a loss in one year
all partners, or all but one, are declared insolvent
one partner goes on a long trip abroad
a new partner is admitted to the firm with the consent of every existing partner
explanation: Compulsory dissolution happens when continuing becomes impossible or unlawful, such as the insolvency of all or all but one partner, or the business becoming illegal. A loss in one year or admitting a partner does not end the firm.

stem: A joint stock company is
options: an informal association that needs no registration
a group of partners who share unlimited liability
a business owned by one person with limited liability
an artificial person created by law with a separate legal entity
explanation: A company is formed by registration under the companies law and becomes a legal person separate from its members; it can own property and sue in its own name. Unlimited liability belongs to ordinary partnerships.

stem: "Perpetual succession" of a company means that
options: the eldest son of a director automatically becomes a director when his father dies
profits are kept forever and never paid as dividends
the company continues to exist even if its members change or die
the company's shares can never be sold to outsiders
explanation: Because the company is a separate legal person, its life does not depend on its members; shares change hands and the company continues. It has nothing to do with inheriting directorships.

stem: In Pakistan, companies are registered with, and regulated by, the
options: Federal Board of Revenue
Pakistan Stock Exchange
State Bank of Pakistan
Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan
explanation: The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) registers companies through its company registry and regulates them. The State Bank regulates banks, and the stock exchange is a market for securities, not a registrar.

stem: The liability of a shareholder in a company limited by shares is
options: fixed by the directors after each loss
limited to the unpaid amount, if any, on the shares he holds
equal to the total debts of the company
unlimited, like that of a partner in an ordinary partnership firm under the 1932 Act
explanation: A shareholder can be asked to pay only what remains unpaid on his shares; once they are fully paid, he owes nothing more for the company's debts. Unlimited liability is the position of partners.

stem: The document that defines a company's name, registered office, objects and the liability of its members is the
options: prospectus
partnership deed
memorandum of association
articles of association
explanation: The memorandum is the company's charter; it states what the company is and what it can do, and it governs its relations with outsiders. The articles contain internal rules of management.

stem: The articles of association of a company mainly contain
options: an invitation to the public to buy shares
the objects for which the company is formed
the certificate that brings the company into being
rules for the internal management of the company
explanation: Articles deal with matters such as meetings, voting, the appointment of directors and transfer of shares. The objects are set out in the memorandum.

stem: A company comes into existence as a legal person on the date shown on its
options: certificate of incorporation
articles of association
first share certificate
prospectus
explanation: On registration, the registrar issues a certificate of incorporation, and from that date the company is a legal entity. A prospectus is issued later, if the company invites the public to buy shares.

stem: A prospectus is issued by a public company to
options: lay down the rules for meetings of directors
record the minutes of the annual general meeting of shareholders for the registrar
invite the public to subscribe for its shares or debentures
prove that the company has been registered
explanation: A prospectus gives details of the company and the securities offered so that the public can decide whether to invest. Rules for meetings appear in the articles.

stem: Under the doctrine of ultra vires, an act of a company that is beyond the objects in its memorandum is
options: valid if it earns a profit for the company
void, and cannot be made valid even if all members approve it
valid, provided the directors approve it at a board meeting
voidable at the choice of the company's creditors
explanation: An act outside the memorandum's objects is beyond the company's legal powers and is void from the start; even unanimous approval by shareholders cannot ratify it. Approval by directors or the profit earned makes no difference.

stem: The doctrine of constructive notice means that anyone dealing with a company is
options: required to inspect the company's accounts before dealing
presumed to know the contents of its memorandum and articles
protected against all acts of the directors
entitled to assume that internal rules have been followed
explanation: Because the memorandum and articles are public documents, outsiders are treated as knowing what they contain. The right to assume internal procedures were followed is the separate doctrine of indoor management.

stem: A supplier dealing in good faith with a company is entitled to assume that its internal procedures, such as passing a needed resolution, have been properly followed. This is the doctrine of
options: constructive notice
ultra vires
indoor management
perpetual succession
explanation: The doctrine of indoor management protects outsiders who cannot see into the company's internal affairs. Constructive notice works the other way, presuming outsiders know the public documents.

stem: Persons who conceive the idea of a company and take the steps needed to form it are called
options: directors
debenture holders
promoters
auditors
explanation: Promoters find the business opportunity, arrange the capital and prepare documents for registration. Directors are appointed to manage the company once it exists.

stem: A key difference between a private and a public company is that a private company
options: does not need to be registered under the companies law
must have at least seven directors on its board and publish a prospectus each year
cannot invite the general public to subscribe for its shares
has unlimited liability for all its members
explanation: A private company restricts the transfer of its shares and is not allowed to offer them to the public; a public company can issue a prospectus. Both are registered and both can have limited liability.

stem: The holders of ordinary shares in a company are
options: its bankers, entitled to repayment on demand
its owners, with voting rights and a varying dividend
its employees, entitled to a fixed monthly wage
its creditors, entitled to fixed interest every year
explanation: Ordinary shareholders own the company, vote at meetings and receive whatever dividend the directors declare from profits. Creditors who earn fixed interest are debenture holders.

stem: Preference shareholders have priority over ordinary shareholders in
options: voting at every general meeting of the company
receiving all of the profit that is left after paying expenses and taxes each year
payment of a fixed dividend and return of capital on winding up
electing the board of directors each year
explanation: Preference shares carry a fixed rate of dividend that is paid before any ordinary dividend, and capital is repaid to them first on winding up. They usually do not have normal voting rights.

stem: For cumulative preference shares, a dividend not paid in a loss-making year
options: is carried forward and paid in a later year before ordinary dividends
lapses and is never paid to the shareholders
is paid by the directors from their own pockets
is converted into ordinary shares at once
explanation: With cumulative preference shares, unpaid dividends accumulate as arrears that must be cleared before ordinary shareholders receive anything. For non-cumulative preference shares, the unpaid dividend lapses.

stem: A debenture holder of a company is
options: an owner of the company who shares in its profits through dividends each year
a member who votes at the annual general meeting
a creditor who lends money and receives a fixed rate of interest
a director who receives a monthly fee
explanation: A debenture is an acknowledgement of a loan to the company; its holder earns interest whether or not the company makes a profit. Shareholders, not debenture holders, own the company and receive dividends.

stem: Shares issued free of charge to existing shareholders out of a company's accumulated profits are called
options: right shares
bonus shares
preference shares
sweat equity shares
explanation: Bonus shares capitalise reserves: shareholders receive extra shares without paying for them. Right shares are offered to existing shareholders but must be paid for.

stem: When a company offers new shares first to its existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings, it is making a
options: right issue
public issue
bonus issue
private placement
explanation: A right issue protects existing shareholders' proportion of ownership, and they pay for the new shares. A bonus issue is free, and a public issue is offered to everyone through a prospectus.

stem: The maximum amount of capital a company is allowed to raise by issuing shares, as stated in its memorandum, is its
options: called-up capital
paid-up capital
authorised capital
issued capital
explanation: Authorised (nominal) capital is the upper limit fixed in the memorandum. Issued capital is the part actually offered to investors, which can be equal to or less than the authorised capital.

stem: A company has issued 100,000 shares of Rs. 10 each and has called Rs. 8 per share. All calls have been received except Rs. 2 per share on 5,000 shares. Its paid-up capital is
explanation: Called-up capital is 100,000 × Rs. 8 = Rs. 800,000. Calls in arrears are 5,000 × Rs. 2 = Rs. 10,000, so paid-up capital is Rs. 790,000. Rs. 800,000 is the called-up amount, before deducting the unpaid calls.

stem: When a company issues a share of face value Rs. 10 for Rs. 12, the extra Rs. 2 is called
options: share discount
dividend
share premium
bonus
explanation: Issuing shares above face value is an issue at a premium; the extra amount goes to a share premium account. A dividend is a share of profit paid to shareholders, not an amount paid by them.

stem: Part of the uncalled capital that a company decides by special resolution will be called only if the company is wound up is
options: subscribed capital
authorised capital
reserve capital
working capital
explanation: Reserve capital is kept back as a safety margin for creditors and can be called only on winding up. Working capital is an accounting idea (current assets less current liabilities), not a class of share capital.

stem: If a shareholder fails to pay a call on his shares after due notice, the company may, if its articles allow,
options: forfeit the shares
issue him bonus shares instead
transfer them to a director free
convert them into debentures
explanation: Forfeiture cancels the shares of a member who fails to pay calls, and the amount already paid is usually lost to him. It must follow the procedure in the articles, including a proper notice.

stem: A resolution passed by a simple majority of votes at a general meeting is an
options: ordinary resolution
unanimous resolution
board resolution
special resolution
explanation: An ordinary resolution needs more votes in favour than against. A special resolution needs a larger majority of at least three-fourths of the votes cast.

stem: A special resolution of a company requires
options: the approval of the board of directors only
the written consent of every single member of the company, including absent members
a simple majority of the members present at the meeting
at least three-fourths of the votes cast by members present and voting
explanation: Special resolutions are needed for major decisions, such as altering the articles, and require a three-fourths majority of votes cast. A simple majority is enough only for an ordinary resolution.

stem: The minimum number of members who must be present for a meeting to transact business validly is the
options: minutes
agenda
proxy
quorum
explanation: Without a quorum, decisions taken at a meeting are invalid. The agenda is the list of business, and minutes are the written record of what was decided.

stem: A person appointed by a shareholder to attend and vote at a general meeting on his behalf is a
options: registrar
proxy
trustee
promoter
explanation: A member who cannot attend may appoint a proxy to vote for him. A promoter takes part in forming the company, not in voting for members.

stem: The annual general meeting of a company is held mainly to
options: prepare the prospectus for a new public issue
settle disputes among partners of the firm
consider the accounts, declare dividends and elect directors
register the company and receive its certificate
explanation: At the AGM, shareholders receive the audited accounts and directors' report, approve dividends, and elect directors and auditors. Registration happens before the company exists, long before any AGM.

stem: A cooperative society is mainly formed to
options: trade in shares on the stock exchange
serve its members rather than to earn maximum profit
carry out government policy as a public enterprise
earn the highest possible profit for a few investors
explanation: A cooperative's chief aim is service: members pool resources to buy, sell or borrow on better terms for themselves. Profit maximisation is the usual aim of companies.

stem: Voting in a cooperative society is based on the principle of
options: one member, one vote, whatever the shares held
votes in proportion to the purchases each member made during the year
one share, one vote, as in a company
votes given only to founding members
explanation: Cooperatives are run democratically: each member has one vote, however much capital he has put in. One share, one vote is the company rule.

stem: A society formed by consumers to buy goods in bulk and sell them to members at fair prices is a
options: consumers' cooperative society
housing cooperative society
producers' cooperative society
credit cooperative society
explanation: A consumers' cooperative cuts out middlemen to supply members with daily goods. A producers' cooperative is formed by small producers to buy raw materials and sell their output.

stem: Farmers in a village join together to borrow money at low interest for seeds and fertiliser. They have formed a
options: joint stock company
credit cooperative society
marketing cooperative society
consumers' cooperative society
explanation: A credit cooperative collects savings and lends to members at reasonable interest, saving them from moneylenders. A marketing cooperative instead helps members sell their produce.

stem: In a cooperative society, surplus that remains after paying a limited dividend on capital is usually distributed
options: to the government as a special tax on the income of all cooperative societies
entirely to the managing committee as a bonus
among members strictly in proportion to the shares they hold
among members in proportion to the business they did with the society
explanation: The patronage bonus rewards members according to their purchases or sales through the society, which reflects the service motive. Dividing all surplus by capital would be the company principle.

stem: A business owned and controlled by the government is called a
options: sole proprietorship
private limited company
cooperative society
public enterprise
explanation: Public enterprises are owned, financed and controlled by the state, at the federal or provincial level. Private companies and sole proprietorships are owned by private individuals.

stem: A public enterprise run directly by a government ministry, financed through the government budget and staffed by civil servants, is a
options: departmental undertaking
holding company
government company
statutory corporation
explanation: A departmental undertaking, such as a railway run by a ministry, is part of the government itself. A statutory corporation is created by a special Act and has its own legal identity.

stem: A public corporation differs from a departmental undertaking mainly because the corporation
options: is managed directly by a ministry's civil servants
is owned by private shareholders who elect its directors at the annual general meeting
is financed only through the annual federal budget
is created by a special Act and has a separate legal entity
explanation: A statutory (public) corporation is set up by its own Act of the legislature, can own property and sue in its own name, and enjoys more operational freedom. Budget finance and ministry control describe a departmental undertaking.

stem: A company in which the government holds at least a majority of the share capital is a
options: partnership firm
departmental undertaking
cooperative society
government company
explanation: A government company is registered under the companies law like any other company, but the state owns the majority of its shares. A departmental undertaking is not a company at all.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a joint stock company?
options: separate legal entity from its members
mutual agency among all its members
limited liability of shareholders
transferability of shares in a public company
explanation: In a company, members are not agents of one another; the company acts through its directors. Mutual agency is a feature of partnership, where each partner can bind the others.

stem: The owner of a sole proprietorship keeps
options: a share decided by his creditors
all the profit of the business
only a salary fixed by law
half the profit, the rest going to the state
explanation: The sole proprietor bears all the risk and so is entitled to all the profit. Sharing profit is a feature of partnership.

stem: A partner who is not known to the public as a partner but takes an active part in the business is a
options: secret partner
nominal partner
minor partner
sleeping partner
explanation: A secret partner manages the business but his partnership is hidden from outsiders. A nominal partner is the opposite: publicly known but with no real role.

stem: Admitting a new partner to an existing firm generally requires
options: the consent of all the existing partners
the consent of the senior partner only
the approval of the registrar of firms
a special resolution of shareholders
explanation: Because partnership rests on mutual trust and agency, no person can be introduced as a partner without the consent of all partners, unless the deed provides otherwise. Special resolutions belong to companies.

stem: A company's relations with outsiders and its permitted activities are set out in its
options: share certificate
partnership deed
memorandum of association
articles of association
explanation: The memorandum states the company's objects and powers, which outsiders deal with. The articles concern internal management.

stem: Dividends on ordinary shares are
options: paid every year whether or not there is a profit
fixed in advance at the time the shares are issued
paid before the preference dividend, as ordinary shares carry the first right to profit
paid out of profits at a rate recommended by the directors
explanation: Ordinary dividends vary with profit and are paid only after the preference dividend. A fixed rate in advance is a feature of preference shares.

stem: Interest on debentures must be paid
options: only if the company makes a profit that year
even if the company makes a loss in that year
only after all the dividends to shareholders have been declared and paid
only when shareholders vote to pay it
explanation: Debenture interest is a charge on the company, owed to creditors regardless of profit. Dividends, by contrast, depend on profits.

stem: Debentures that are secured by a charge on the company's assets are called
options: convertible debentures
bearer debentures
naked debentures
secured or mortgage debentures
explanation: Secured (mortgage) debentures give holders a claim on specified assets if the company fails to pay. Naked debentures carry no such security.

stem: Preference shares that the company can buy back after a fixed period or at its option are called
options: redeemable preference shares
participating preference shares
convertible preference shares
cumulative preference shares
explanation: Redeemable preference shares are repaid by the company under the terms of issue. Convertible preference shares are instead changed into ordinary shares.

stem: A cooperative society is managed by
options: a board appointed by the State Bank
the member with the largest share capital
a committee elected by its members
the government officer who registered it
explanation: Democratic management is a basic cooperative principle: members elect a managing committee. Control by the largest investor would contradict one member, one vote.

stem: Which form of business is most suitable for a small grocery shop in a town?
options: statutory corporation
public limited company
sole proprietorship
government company
explanation: A small shop needs little capital and gains from quick decisions and personal service, which suits a sole proprietor. Public companies and corporations are for large-scale undertakings.

stem: A company that controls another company by holding more than half of its voting shares is a
options: private firm
subsidiary company
cooperative company
holding company
explanation: The controlling company is the holding company; the one controlled is its subsidiary. A cooperative is a different form of organisation altogether.

stem: A sleeping partner is liable to the firm's creditors
options: only up to the profits he has received
fully, in the same way as the active partners
only if he is also a nominal partner
not at all, since he takes no part in management
explanation: Not taking part in management does not reduce a partner's liability: a sleeping partner is liable without limit for the firm's debts. Only a minor admitted to benefits has limited liability.
